source_paper.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the understanding from the paper that oxidation processes in HEAs are strongly linked to microstructural features and diffusive pathways (e.g., as seen in the discussion of non-uniform oxide layers and element diffusion in PMC11169556::web::009 and ::web::010), combined with knowledge from additive manufacturing literature.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the discussion of oxidation kinetics by addressing the role of additive manufacturing-induced residual stresses and grain boundary network in degradation, proposing a specific post-process treatment (HIP) not considered in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Degradation originates from microstructural inhomogeneities and residual stresses inherent to the additive manufacturing process, which promote localized fast-path oxidation along high-angle grain boundaries and columnar grain features. Post-process hot isostatic pressing (HIP) can alleviate these defects, resulting in more uniform oxide scale formation and enhanced resistance to degradation under both oxidizing and reducing environments.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix that contains residual stresses, anisotropic columnar grains, and inhomogeneous grain boundaries typical of AM processes.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a tailored hot isostatic pressing (HIP) treatment (e.g. at ~900°C under high pressure for a short duration) designed to reduce residual stresses and refine grain structure without compromising the high-temperature phase stability.
hypothesis.conditions: Test the HIP-treated and as-built samples under elevated-temperature exposures (e.g. 400°C) in both oxidizing and reducing gas environments for equivalent durations, monitoring oxide scale development and degradation behavior.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Reduction in grain boundary misorientation and residual stress fields, leading to a more homogeneous microstructure with fewer fast diffusion paths for oxygen ingress.
hypothesis.mechanism: In additively manufactured alloys, residual stresses and columnar grain structures create localized regions with high energy that act as preferential sites for rapid oxidation and crack initiation (consistent with general knowledge on grain boundary diffusion and surface degradation, see supporting co-occurrence in MatKG and materials texts). HIP treatment relaxes these residual stresses and homogenizes the grain structure, reducing the density of fast diffusion paths. Consequently, the protective oxide scale that forms becomes more uniform, with less localized buildup and reduced propensity for spallation or accelerated degradation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: HIP-treated samples are expected to exhibit a more uniform, adherent oxide scale, reduced localized degradation features, and lower overall oxidation rates compared to untreated specimens. The improvement should be appreciable through reduced crack density and more consistent oxide thickness.
hypothesis.baseline: As-built additively manufactured samples exhibiting inhomogeneous microstructure and higher residual stresses.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism applies to conditions where the microstructural effects and residual stress dominate the oxidation kinetics, typically at moderate temperatures (~400°C) before any bulk phase transformations occur.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement is subject to processing parameters and may vary; however, the qualitative trend of enhanced oxide uniformity is expected.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of the alloy: one as-built by additive manufacturing and one subjected to the proposed HIP treatment. Expose both sets to identical elevated-temperature oxidizing (and separate reducing) conditions (e.g., 400°C, fixed time, known partial pressures). Characterize the surface oxide using TEM, EBSD (to check microstructure), and oxidation rate measurements (e.g., weight gain/loss).

Residual stress via X-ray diffraction
Oxide scale uniformity and adhesion via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HIP-treated samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in oxide uniformity, lower oxidation rates, or reduced crack densities relative to the as-built samples, the hypothesis that microstructural inhomogeneities and residual stresses control degradation (and can be ameliorated by HIP) would be falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: This hypothesis applies established superalloy principles—where microalloying with elements like Nb improves oxide scale stability by reducing grain boundary diffusion—to a novel, compositionally complex HEA system.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Trace Nb Microalloying Promotes Grain Boundary Segregation in the Oxide Scale to Inhibit Degradation
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As‐built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix produced by plasma arc additive manufacturing.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a trace amount (approximately 0.2 wt.%) of Nb into the feedstock powder during alloy preparation, ensuring that bulk phase stability (FCC matrix) is maintained.
hypothesis.conditions: Prepare two sets of samples—one with the baseline composition and one with the Nb-doped composition. Expose both sets to elevated temperatures (650–750 °C) in oxidizing and mildly reducing environments for comparable durations.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Nb segregates preferentially to the grain boundaries of the evolving oxide scale, which then reduces intergranular oxygen diffusion and stabilizes the scale against spallation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Nb is known from superalloy research to segregate to oxide grain boundaries where it delays oxygen diffusion along fast paths. In this HEA, the trace Nb will migrate during high-temperature exposure to decorate the grain boundaries of the nascent multicomponent oxide scale, thereby reducing grain boundary diffusivity and limiting rapid oxidation. This helps control the pace of scale growth and improves high-temperature stability without substantially altering the mechanical properties of the bulk alloy.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Nb-doped samples should display significantly reduced oxide scale thickness, lower mass gain, and enhanced adhesion of the oxide layer compared to the baseline alloy. The improvements are expected to be clearly measurable, although exact quantitative advantage requires experimental determination.
hypothesis.baseline: The undoped HEA, which forms an oxide scale governed solely by its inherent multicomponent alloy chemistry and may develop faster oxidation kinetics via uninhibited grain boundary diffusion.
hypothesis.boundary: The Nb concentration must remain low (around 0.2 wt.%) to avoid altering the primary FCC phase and mechanical properties, and exposure conditions should be within the 650–750 °C range to stimulate Nb segregation without triggering additional phase transformations.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While Nb's role in oxide scale stabilization is documented in simpler systems, its precise effectiveness in this complex HEA is uncertain and will require systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA samples—one baseline and one with 0.2 wt.% Nb addition—using identical plasma arc additive manufacturing conditions. Expose both sample sets to 700 °C in synthetic air and a mild reducing atmosphere for a predetermined time. Analyze the oxide scale using TEM/EDS to check for Nb segregation at grain boundaries, quantify mass gain (TGA), and perform adhesion tests (e.g., scratch tests) on the oxide layer.
measurements: Presence and distribution of Nb in the oxide scale (TEM/EDS)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (SEM/TEM, XRD)
Mass gain during high-temperature exposure (TGA)
Oxide adhesion strength (scratch testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped samples do not show significant Nb segregation at the oxide grain boundaries or if the oxidation kinetics (oxide thickness, mass gain, and adhesion) are not statistically improved over the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples do not show a significantly lower degradation rate (e.g., oxide scale continuity, lower internal oxidation) in oxidizing conditions compared to controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: Selective electron beam melting of Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 high entropy alloys using elemental powder blend.

hypotheses.builds_on: This approach integrates principles from superalloy design where reactive elements are used to stabilize protective oxides, expanding on the paper’s observations of microstructural inhomogeneities in additively manufactured HEAs.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces hafnium as a novel minor addition to directly target problematic oxidation nucleation sites, offering an alternative mechanism to improve degradation resistance in the fcc HEA that was not proposed in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Minor Hafnium Addition to Stabilize Surface Precipitates and Mitigate Localized Oxidation
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix produced by additive manufacturing, which may contain nano-scale precipitates or inclusions acting as heterogeneous nucleation sites for oxidation.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a small addition (approximately 0.5–1 at.%) of hafnium (Hf) into the elemental powder blend during the additive manufacturing process.
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) under both oxidizing and moderately reducing gas environments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation of Hf-rich precipitates near grain boundaries and at internal interfaces that act to pin microstructural defects and modify local oxidation kinetics.
hypothesis.mechanism: Hafnium has a high oxygen affinity and forms stable, finely dispersed HfO₂ particles when exposed to oxygen. By incorporating a minor amount of Hf, these particles can preferentially form at sites that would otherwise serve as active regions for rapid oxidation initiation (such as nano-precipitates or inclusions). The presence of stable HfO₂ can act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion and reduce the formation of non-uniform oxide regions, thereby mitigating localized degradation without significantly altering the bulk fcc microstructure.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Hf-doped samples should show a more uniform oxide scale with reduced spallation, lower overall oxidation-induced weight gain, and fewer localized degradation sites compared to undoped controls, particularly under oxidizing conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: As-built HEA without any Hf addition, potentially exhibiting heterogeneous oxide nucleation from existing inclusions or precipitates.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated under oxidizing conditions where Hf can form stable oxides; under purely reducing conditions the impact might be minimal, and care must be taken to maintain overall mechanical performance.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise effective concentration of Hf and its distribution within the microstructure remain to be optimized, and possible interactions with other alloying elements need careful monitoring.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two batches of samples: one with the standard composition and one with 0.5–1 at.% Hf addition. Subject both the sets to 700–900 °C in an oxidizing environment. Use TEM/EDS, along with SEM and weight gain measurements, to characterize the oxide scale morphology, identify the presence and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates, and assess oxidation kinetics.
measurements: Weight gain during exposure
High-resolution microscopy (TEM/EDS) for precipitate and oxide scale characterization
Surface spallation or adhesion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in terms of reduced oxidation-induced degradation and enhanced oxide scale uniformity compared to the undoped baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Plasma Arc Robot for Direct Wall High-Entropy Alloy Additive Manufacturing.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observation that microstructural refinement and thermal history affect oxidation behavior in plasma arc–fabricated HEAs (PMC12843301::web::017, PMC12843301::web::024), combined with principles of protective alloying element enrichment from superalloy studies (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a rapid cyclic thermal post-treatment to deliberately induce near‐surface Cr/Al segregation—an approach not previously applied to this HEA—to form a self‐passivating, protective oxide scale without compromising the bulk FCC matrix and its mechanical integrity.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Rapid Cyclic Thermal Post‐Treatment Induces Near-Surface Cr/Al Enrichment to Form a Protective Oxide Scale
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As‐built, plasma arc–fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix and dendritic/columnar microstructure.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the alloy to a series of short, high‐temperature cycles (e.g., 5 minutes at ~750 °C followed by rapid cooling) in an inert or low‐oxygen atmosphere before exposure to service conditions.
hypothesis.conditions: Cycles performed in an inert gas (e.g., high-purity argon) followed by subsequent exposure at 650–750 °C in oxidizing (synthetic air) or reducing gas environments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enrichment of Cr and Al in the near‐surface region due to differential diffusivities during rapid thermal cycling.
hypothesis.mechanism: During the brief high-temperature pulses, elements with higher mobility—specifically Cr and Al—migrate preferentially to the surface. This enriched layer then, upon subsequent high‐temperature exposure, forms a thin, adherent Cr/Al‐rich oxide that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and further degradation. This approach leverages kinetic differences in the multicomponent system without triggering bulk phase changes.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to as‐built samples, thermally pre‐treated specimens will exhibit a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale with lower mass gain, thereby slowing the degradation rate. The improvement is expected to be moderate, though the precise magnitude depends on cycle parameters.
hypothesis.baseline: The as‐built HEA that, when exposed directly, develops a less controlled oxide scale with potential spallation or nonuniform growth due to its inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
hypothesis.boundary: Thermal cycle peak temperatures (around 750 °C) and durations must be optimized to induce surface segregation without altering the FCC bulk microstructure or causing unwanted phase transformations.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimum cycle number, duration, and temperature are uncertain and require experimental calibration to ensure effective surface enrichment without deleterious effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from identically produced as‐built HEA. Apply the rapid cyclic thermal treatment to one set while leaving the other untreated. Then expose both sets to 700 °C in synthetic air for a fixed duration. Use surface analysis techniques (e.g., XPS and SEM-EDS) to quantify Cr/Al surface enrichment, measure oxide scale thickness via cross-sectional SEM/TEM, and record mass gain with thermogravimetric analysis.
measurements: Surface elemental composition and segregation profiles (XPS, EDS)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (SEM/TEM)
Mass gain during oxidation (TGA)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated samples do not show statistically significant Cr/Al enrichment at the surface, or if the resulting oxide scales are not thinner, more uniform, and accompanied by lower mass gain compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Design and Fabrication of New High Entropy Alloys for Evaluating Titanium Replacements in Additive Manufacturing.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that additive manufacturing enables site‐specific microstructural control and oxidation behavior influenced by elemental constituents, as discussed in the paper regarding HEA fabrication and characterization (PMC7372361).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s processing insights by pre-forming a protective oxide scale to decouple degradation pathways under oxidizing conditions without compromising the alloy’s integrity.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Protective oxide scale formation from selective oxidation of Al and Cr governs degradation under oxidizing conditions.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix and a relatively pristine surface.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to develop a continuous, dual-layer oxide scale enriched in Al2O3 and Cr2O3 before subjecting samples to prolonged high-temperature oxidizing exposure.
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) in controlled oxidizing gas environments (with defined oxygen partial pressure) for defined exposure durations.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A protective, adherent oxide scale that forms heterogeneously yet continuously on the alloy surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: At high temperatures, the inherent presence of aluminum and chromium promotes selective oxidation to form a composite oxide scale. This scale, by virtue of its low ionic diffusivity and excellent adhesion, impedes further oxygen ingress. In oxidizing environments, the integrity of this scale slows down further degradation. Under reducing conditions, however, the scale’s composition can change or be partially reduced, diminishing its protectiveness. Thus, the scale’s nature and adherence govern the long-term stability of the alloy without compromising the FCC matrix’s mechanical integrity.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit lower weight gain and reduced oxide scale thickening vs. non-treated samples when exposed to oxidizing high-temperature environments. A substantial protective effect (direction: improvement in oxidation resistance) is expected, although the precise magnitude is moderately uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: Degradation behavior of as-built, untreated alloy surfaces under similar exposures.
hypothesis.boundary: Effectiveness is expected only in environments with sufficiently high oxygen partial pressures and temperatures where selective oxidation is active; in reducing atmospheres the beneficial oxide may be compromised.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Moderate uncertainty exists in scale adhesion variations and potential scale spallation effects at the upper end of the temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one pre-oxidized to form the protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale and one untreated control. Expose both sets to identical oxidizing conditions (700–900 °C, fixed oxygen partial pressure) for set durations.
measurements: Weight gain analysis via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)
Surface oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM/EDS
Adhesion and continuity of the oxide via scratch testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit lower weight gain, thinner and more adherent oxide scales, or if differences in degradation rates relative to untreated samples are not statistically significant, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Oxidation Behavior of Refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding in the paper that degradation is linked to oxygen ingress through microstructural defects (e.g., cracks at the oxide-metal interface) in high-entropy alloys.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a post-processing heat treatment to tailor the microstructure (i.e., grain size) of a non-refractory, fcc high‐entropy alloy to specifically reduce grain boundary density and hence mitigate degradation, a route not examined in the referenced study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Post‐processing grain growth in the additively manufactured alloy reduces high-angle grain boundary density, thus mitigating rapid oxygen ingress through intergranular paths that initiate scale cracking and degradation during elevated-temperature exposure in oxidizing atmospheres.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a fine-scale, non-equilibrium microstructure typical of additive manufacturing.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled high-temperature annealing (subsolidus, e.g., 900–950 °C for several hours) to promote modest grain growth and reduce high-energy intergranular defects without inducing unwanted phase transformations.
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 700–800 °C) in an oxidizing gas environment (static air) for durations comparable to service conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Reduced density of fast diffusion paths (grain boundaries) leading to a more continuous and adherent oxide layer with lower porosity.
hypothesis.mechanism: Coarser grains lead to fewer grain boundary channels for oxygen diffusion. With reduced oxygen ingress, formation of unprotective or volatile oxides (e.g., transient Cr or Ti oxides) is minimized and the protective oxide scale remains intact. This effect builds on the paper’s identification of scale cracking and oxygen ingress through defects as degradation triggers.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A lower mass gain per unit area and a more coherent, less porous oxide scale compared to the as-built condition, with a reduction in scale spallation evident over similar exposure times. The improvement is expected to be moderate but significant under the chosen exposure conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-built alloy exhibiting a fine, high defect density microstructure leading to faster degradation as evidenced by the evolution of porosity and spallation under oxidation (akin to crack propagation observed in the refractory HEA studied in the paper).
hypothesis.boundary: The intervention should not be so severe as to coarsen grains excessively or promote undesirable phase transformations that compromise the alloy’s overall mechanical integrity.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is uncertain because the optimal balance between grain size and mechanical properties must be calibrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one as-built and one subjected to the proposed annealing heat treatment. Expose both sets to elevated-temperature oxidation (e.g., 750 °C in static air) for a fixed time. Characterize mass gain, oxide scale morphology (SEM) and adherence.
measurements: Mass gain per cm²
SEM imaging of oxide scale thickness and porosity
XRD phase analysis of oxides
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale porosity and mass gain compared to as-built samples, or if scale cracking remains unmitigated, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: Selective electron beam melting of Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 high entropy alloys using elemental powder blend.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation of significant Al evaporation during SEBM processing informs the idea that compensating for such loss can maintain adequate levels of protective elements.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a deliberate adjustment of initial powder composition to preempt evaporative depletion—a strategy tailored specifically for the fcc HEA system that was not examined in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Compensatory Doping to Offset Evaporative Losses for Improved Protective Oxide Scale Formation
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix produced by additive manufacturing using nominal elemental ratios.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the initial powder feedstock by adding approximately 5 at.% extra Al (and/or a modest extra amount of Cr if needed) relative to the nominal design to compensate for evaporation losses during processing.
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere (such as air or a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A sustained availability of protective elements at the alloy’s surface that fosters the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (predominantly Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃).
hypothesis.mechanism: During the SEBM process it has been observed that significant evaporation of light elements (notably Al) occurs. This evaporation may lead to locally depleted concentrations of Al (and possibly Cr), which are critical to forming a protective oxide barrier. By pre-emptively adding extra Al to the powder blend, after processing the surface retains sufficient Al to form a uniform and adherent oxide layer. The improved oxide scale serves as a barrier to further oxygen ingress during high-temperature exposure, thereby mitigating oxidation-induced degradation while preserving the fcc matrix and mechanical integrity.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the compensatory-doped samples should exhibit lower weight gain during oxidation tests, a more uniform and continuous oxide scale (as confirmed by SEM/EPMA), and fewer spallation features.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-built HEA produced with the nominal composition (without compensatory doping), which is susceptible to elemental depletion by evaporation.
hypothesis.boundary: This improvement is expected to be significant under oxidizing conditions; under reducing conditions, where oxide formation is minimal, the effect may be less pronounced.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal extra doping level is uncertain and may require refinement; interactions between extra Al and other elements in the fcc matrix need to be monitored to ensure mechanical properties remain uncompromised.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of samples: one with the conventional nominal composition and one with ~5 at.% extra Al (and additional Cr if needed). Subject both sets to 700–900 °C in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere for equivalent time durations. Characterize the surface oxide scale via SEM/EPMA, measure weight gain over time, and perform adhesion/spallation tests on the oxide scale.
measurements: Weight change (gain) during exposure
Microscopic (SEM/EPMA) evaluation of oxide scale continuity and thickness
Adhesion or spallation index of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the compensatory-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale uniformity (fewer spalls and cracks) and reduced weight gain compared to the nominal baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The finding in the paper that ultrafine-grained microstructure enhances oxidation resistance by promoting protective oxide scale formation [PMC9026100].
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the concept of microstructural refinement to additively manufactured HEAs specifically and proposes using SMAT as a controlled post-processing step to mitigate degradation under oxidizing conditions, an aspect not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Surface grain refinement via post‐processing (e.g., shot peening/SMAT) promotes rapid diffusion of Cr and Al to form a continuous protective oxide scale, thereby mitigating degradation during high-temperature oxidation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a relatively coarse as-built surface microstructure and fcc matrix.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) to the top few hundred microns to induce ultrafine-grained microstructure.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose the treated and untreated specimens to oxidizing gas environments at temperatures between 850 °C and 1050 °C for 100 hours.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density and elevated surface free energy in the SMAT-treated region.
hypothesis.mechanism: The ultrafine-grained surface provides enhanced short-circuit diffusion paths for Cr and Al, which leads to the preferential early formation of continuous, adherent protective Cr2O3 and Al2O3 layers that inhibit further oxidation and associated degradation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxide scale growth rate (mass gain reduced by approximately 30–50% relative to the untreated baseline) and fewer oxide scale cracks or spallation events.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated additively manufactured HEA with its original grain structure tested under the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: Effective for oxidation exposures within the temperature range 850–1050 °C and oxidation durations on the order of 100 hours.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the trend is supported by prior work on microstructural refinement [PMC9026100::web::018], the quantitative reduction may vary based on the degree of refinement achievable in additively manufactured samples.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one subjected to SMAT to refine the surface microstructure and one left as-built. Expose both sets to identical oxidizing conditions (850–1050 °C for 100 h) and compare oxidation kinetics, oxide scale composition, and morphology.
measurements: Mass gain (mg/cm²) over time
Phase identification via XRD and cross-sectional SEM/EDS of the oxide layers
Grain size and defect density characterization (e.g., EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SMAT-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate and do not form a thinner, more protective oxide scale compared to the untreated specimens, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
